protocols.name: CTAB genomic DNA extraction (fungal mycelium / plant tissue)
protocols.pr: CTAB detergent lyses cells and complexes with nucleic acids; chloroform removes proteins and polysaccharides, and isopropanol precipitates the DNA.
mat: Mortar & pestle, liquid nitrogen or sterile sand
st: Grind 100 mg fresh mycelium/leaf tissue to a fine powder in liquid nitrogen (or with sterile sand).
Transfer to a 2 mL tube with 800 μL pre-warmed CTAB buffer; mix by inversion.
Incubate at 65 °C for 45–60 min in the water bath, inverting every 10–15 min.
Cool briefly, add an equal volume of chloroform : isoamyl alcohol (24:1) and mix gently by inversion for 5 min.
Centrifuge at 12,000 rpm for 10 min at 4 °C; transfer the upper aqueous phase to a fresh tube without disturbing the interface.
Add 0.6 volume chilled isopropanol, mix gently and keep at −20 °C for 30 min (or overnight).
Centrifuge at 12,000 rpm for 10 min; discard supernatant carefully, keeping the pellet.
Wash the pellet with 500 μL chilled 70% ethanol; spin 5 min, drain and air-dry until translucent.
Dissolve in 50–100 μL TE buffer; add RNase A (10 μg/mL) and incubate 37 °C for 30 min if RNA-free DNA is needed.
Check quality on a 0.8% agarose gel and store at −20 °C.
protocols.note: Chloroform work near a flame is dangerous — use in a ventilated area. Never vortex after lysis; genomic DNA shears. β-mercaptoethanol only in the fume hood.

protocols.name: PCR amplification of the ITS region (ITS1/ITS4)
protocols.pr: The internal transcribed spacer of rDNA is amplified with universal primers ITS1 and ITS4 for fungal identification by sequencing.
st: Thaw reagents on ice; prepare master mix for (n + 10%) reactions using the Formulations/Calculators tab.
Per 25 μL reaction: 2.5 μL 10× buffer, 0.5 μL dNTPs, 1 μL each primer, 0.2 μL Taq, 18.8 μL water, 1 μL template.
Dispense master mix, add template last; include a no-template control (NTC).
Spin briefly and load into the thermal cycler.
Programme: 94 °C 5 min; 35 cycles of 94 °C 30 s, 55 °C 45 s, 72 °C 1 min; final 72 °C 7 min; hold 4 °C.
Resolve 5 μL of product on a 1.2% agarose gel; expect ~550–600 bp for most fungi.
Store products at −20 °C or send for sequencing.
protocols.note: Set up reactions in the pre-PCR area with filter tips. An amplicon in the NTC means contamination — discard reagents and repeat.

protocols.name: Agarose gel electrophoresis of DNA
protocols.pr: DNA is negatively charged and migrates towards the anode through an agarose matrix; smaller fragments travel faster, allowing size separation.
mat: Nucleic acid stain (EtBr 0.5 μg/mL or safe dye)
Gel tank, power pack, UV transilluminator
st: Prepare the required percentage gel (0.8% genomic; 1.2–2% PCR products) using the recipe calculator.
Melt agarose in 1× TAE in the microwave in short bursts; swirl between bursts.
Cool to ~55 °C, add stain, pour into the casting tray with comb, and let set 30 min.
Place the gel in the tank, wells to the cathode (black); submerge in 1× TAE by 3–5 mm.
Mix samples with loading dye and load; include a ladder in one lane.
Run at 80–100 V until the tracking dye reaches two-thirds of the gel.
Switch off the supply, then visualise on the UV transilluminator with a face shield.
protocols.note: EtBr is mutagenic — nitrile gloves and dedicated waste. Never open the tank while the power is on.

protocols.name: qPCR (SYBR Green) reaction setup
protocols.pr: SYBR Green fluoresces on binding double-stranded DNA; fluorescence measured each cycle allows quantification of target from the Cq value.
mat: Optical plate/strips & seals, ice, qPCR system
st: Plan the plate layout: samples, standard dilution series (10-fold), NTC — all in duplicate or triplicate.
On ice, prepare master mix: per 10 μL reaction — 5 μL 2× SYBR mix, 0.4 μL each primer, 3.2 μL water; add 1 μL template last.
Seal with optical film, avoid touching the surface; spin briefly to remove bubbles.
Load with well A1 at the marked corner; run: 95 °C 3 min, then 40 cycles of 95 °C 10 s and 60 °C 30 s, followed by melt curve 65→95 °C.
Check the melt curve for a single peak (specific product); analyse Cq values against the standard curve.
Discard the sealed plate unopened, away from the pre-PCR area.
protocols.note: Efficiency of the standard curve should be 90–110% (slope ≈3.3). Multiple melt peaks mean primer-dimers or non-specific products.

protocols.name: Isolation of fungal pathogens from diseased tissue
protocols.pr: Small segments from the advancing margin of a lesion, surface-sterilised, transferred to nutrient medium yield the pathogen while excluding surface contaminants.
st: Wash the diseased tissue under running tap water to remove soil and debris.
Cut 3–5 mm segments spanning the junction of healthy and diseased tissue.
Surface-sterilise in 1% sodium hypochlorite for 1–2 min (or 0.1% HgCl₂ for 30 s).
Rinse in three changes of sterile distilled water, 1 min each.
Blot dry on sterile paper and plate 4–5 segments per PDA plate, spaced apart.
Incubate at 25 ± 2 °C in the BOD incubator; examine daily from day 2.
Subculture hyphal growth emerging from segments onto fresh PDA for purification.
protocols.note: All transfers inside the laminar flow. HgCl₂ is highly toxic — prefer hypochlorite; never discard HgCl₂ down the drain.

protocols.name: Single spore isolation (pure culture)
protocols.pr: A culture established from one spore is genetically uniform, essential for variability studies and identification.
mat: Inoculation needle, microscope, laminar air flow
st: Prepare a dilute spore suspension in sterile water — faintly cloudy (≈ 10³–10⁴ spores/mL using the spore-count calculator).
Spread 0.1 mL evenly over a dried 2% water agar plate; incubate 12–24 h.
Under the low-power objective (or stereo microscope), locate single germinating spores well separated from others.
Cut out the agar block bearing one germinated spore with a sterile needle.
Transfer the block to a fresh PDA plate; incubate at 25 ± 2 °C.
Verify colony purity and uniformity; repeat if mixed.
protocols.note: Work quickly on water agar — delayed pickup lets colonies merge. For non-sporulating fungi use the hyphal-tip method instead.

protocols.name: Slide mount & identification (lactophenol cotton blue)
protocols.pr: Fungal structures stained with lactophenol cotton blue are examined microscopically for genus/species-level identification.
st: Place a small drop of lactophenol cotton blue on a clean slide.
With a sterile needle, tease out a small tuft of mycelium (with spores) from the colony edge.
Spread it gently in the stain; avoid clumping.
Lower a coverslip at an angle to exclude air bubbles.
Examine at 10× then 40×; record hyphae, conidiophores, conidia shape, septation and measurements.
Compare with standard keys; photograph if the microscope has a camera.
protocols.note: Lactophenol contains phenol — avoid skin contact. Seal semi-permanent mounts with nail varnish to keep them for weeks.

protocols.name: Preservation of fungal cultures (slants & oil overlay)
protocols.pr: Reduced metabolism on slants under mineral oil, or refrigeration, keeps cultures viable for months to years without frequent transfer.
st: Inoculate PDA slants with the pure culture and incubate at 25 ± 2 °C until well grown (5–7 days).
For routine storage, keep grown slants at 4 °C in the refrigerator; transfer every 3–6 months.
For long-term storage, pour sterile liquid paraffin over the grown slant to 1 cm above the agar tip.
Label with culture code, species, host, date; seal caps with parafilm.
Store oiled slants upright at room temperature or 4 °C; revive by picking mycelium from beneath the oil onto fresh PDA.
protocols.note: Autoclave the paraffin twice on successive days to ensure sterility. Maintain a register matching codes to the culture catalogue.

protocols.name: Pathogenicity test / Koch's postulates (soil-borne fungi)
protocols.pr: Re-establishing disease in a healthy host with the pure isolate, then re-isolating the same fungus, proves the isolate is the causal pathogen.
mat: Pure culture of the test isolate
Sorghum/maize seed or sand-maize meal for mass multiplication
Healthy seed of the susceptible host
st: Mass-multiply the isolate on autoclaved sorghum grains (soaked, twice-autoclaved) for 10–15 days at 25 ± 2 °C.
Mix the inoculum into sterilised soil (typically 2–5% w/w) and fill pots; keep uninoculated sterilised soil as control.
Sow surface-sterilised seeds of the susceptible cultivar; maintain in the glasshouse with normal watering.
Observe regularly and record symptom development (e.g. dry root rot: yellowing, drying, shredded root bark with sclerotia).
Express incidence/severity against controls, which must remain healthy.
Re-isolate the fungus from symptomatic tissue and confirm it matches the original culture morphologically/molecularly.
protocols.note: Include enough replications (≥3 pots per treatment). For Macrophomina dry root rot, moisture stress after flowering accentuates symptom expression.

protocols.name: Poisoned food technique (in-vitro fungicide evaluation)
protocols.pr: Fungicide incorporated into the medium at known concentrations inhibits radial growth; per cent inhibition over control measures fungitoxicity.
mat: Test pathogen culture (5 mm discs from 7-day colony margin)
st: Calculate the fungicide quantity for each required concentration (ppm calculator; account for a.i. %).
Add fungicide to molten PDA at ~45 °C, mix thoroughly, and pour ~20 mL per plate; keep unamended PDA as control.
Once set, place a 5 mm mycelial disc (from the colony margin) at the centre of each plate, inverted mycelium-down.
Incubate at 25 ± 2 °C with ≥3 replications per concentration.
Measure colony diameter (two perpendicular readings) when the control plate is nearly full.
Per cent inhibition I = (C − T)/C × 100, where C and T are control and treatment growth; compute ED₅₀ if needed.
protocols.note: Add fungicide only after the medium cools to ~45 °C, or heat-labile compounds degrade. Use separate pipettes per fungicide to avoid carry-over.

protocols.name: Dual culture technique (antagonist screening)
protocols.pr: Pathogen and antagonist grown on the same plate reveal antibiosis or competition as inhibition of pathogen growth towards the antagonist.
mat: Pathogen and antagonist cultures (Trichoderma, Pseudomonas etc.)
st: Place a 5 mm disc of the pathogen 1 cm from one edge of a PDA plate.
Place a 5 mm disc (or streak) of the antagonist 1 cm from the opposite edge, on the same diameter.
Keep plates inoculated with the pathogen alone as control.
Incubate at 25 ± 2 °C; take readings when the control colony approaches full growth.
Measure pathogen radial growth towards the antagonist (T) and in control (C); inhibition % = (C − T)/C × 100.
Record the interaction class (overgrowth, inhibition zone, deadlock) and photograph.
protocols.note: Inoculate the slower-growing organism 24–48 h earlier if growth rates differ widely, so both meet mid-plate.

protocols.name: Seed health testing — standard blotter method
protocols.pr: Seeds incubated on moist blotters under alternating light permit seed-borne fungi to grow and sporulate for identification.
mat: Incubator with NUV/alternating light if available
st: Soak three blotter layers in sterile water and drain excess; place in sterile plates.
Plate 10 seeds per 9 cm plate (25 for larger plates), evenly spaced; 400 seeds per sample as per ISTA.
Incubate at 22 ± 2 °C under alternating 12 h light/dark for 7 days.
Examine each seed under the stereo microscope from day 5, identifying fungi by habit characters and spores.
Record per cent incidence of each fungus per sample.
Confirm doubtful identities by slide mounts or isolation.
protocols.note: Do not let blotters dry mid-test. Deep-freeze method (−20 °C on day 3 for 24 h) kills germinating seeds if germination obscures readings.

protocols.name: Mechanical sap inoculation of viruses
protocols.pr: Virus in sap enters through micro-wounds made by an abrasive on the leaf surface, establishing infection in the test plant.
mat: Chilled 0.1 M phosphate buffer pH 7.0 (with 0.1% sodium sulphite added fresh)
Pre-chilled mortar & pestle, muslin, cotton swabs
Healthy test plants at the susceptible stage
st: Grind 1 g of young symptomatic tissue in 5–10 mL chilled buffer in a pre-chilled mortar; strain through muslin.
Lightly dust carborundum on the leaves to be inoculated (or add to the sap).
Support a leaf on the palm, dip a swab/pestle in sap and rub gently once or twice from base to tip.
Rinse inoculated leaves with a gentle stream of water after 2–5 min.
Keep plants in an insect-proof glasshouse; include buffer-only controls.
Record symptoms from 5 days onward; confirm infection by ELISA or PCR.
protocols.note: Work fast and keep sap cold — many viruses inactivate in minutes. Wash hands and tools between isolates to prevent cross-contamination.

protocols.name: DAC-ELISA for plant virus detection
protocols.pr: Antigen coated directly on the plate is detected by virus-specific antibody and an enzyme-labelled conjugate; substrate colour indicates virus presence.
mat: Sample extracts, plate reader or visual scoring
st: Extract test samples 1:10 in coating buffer; load 100 μL per well in duplicate; include healthy and positive controls.
Incubate 2 h at 37 °C (or overnight at 4 °C); wash 3× with PBS-T.
Block with 2% skim milk in PBS-T, 1 h at 37 °C; wash 3×.
Add primary antibody at the recommended dilution, 100 μL/well; 1–2 h at 37 °C; wash 3×.
Add alkaline-phosphatase conjugate; 1 h at 37 °C; wash 4×.
Add freshly prepared pNPP (1 mg/mL in 10% diethanolamine pH 9.8); incubate in the dark 30–60 min.
Read A₄₀₅; samples > 2× healthy-control mean are positive.
protocols.note: Never let wells dry between steps. Fresh substrate only; sodium azide in buffers inhibits ALP — exclude it from conjugate/substrate steps.

protocols.name: Composition & use of antioxidant sap-extraction buffer
protocols.pr: Phenolics released on grinding inactivate viruses; antioxidants and chelators in the extraction buffer keep the virus infective and detectable.
mat: Sodium diethyl dithiocarbamate (0.01 M) for phenolic-rich hosts
st: Prepare 0.1 M phosphate buffer pH 7.0 (see Formulations tab) and chill.
Immediately before extraction, add the antioxidant: 0.1 g sodium sulphite per 100 mL, and 0.19 g DIECA per 100 mL for okra/cotton-type hosts.
Use buffer at 2–10 mL per g tissue depending on host succulence.
Grind, strain and use the sap immediately for inoculation or ELISA extraction.
Discard leftover amended buffer; antioxidants do not keep.
protocols.note: DIECA can inhibit some assays downstream — omit for PCR-bound extracts. Match the buffer to the published protocol for your target virus.

protocols.name: Gram staining
protocols.pr: Gram-positive cells retain the crystal violet–iodine complex in their thick peptidoglycan wall after alcohol decolourisation and appear purple; Gram-negative cells lose it and take up the safranin counterstain, appearing pink.
mat: Clean slides, inoculation loop, spirit lamp
Microscope with 100× oil-immersion objective and immersion oil
st: Place a small drop of sterile distilled water on a clean slide; with a flamed, cooled loop pick a small amount of an 18–24 h culture and emulsify to make a thin, even smear.
Air-dry the smear completely, then heat-fix by passing the slide through the flame 2–3 times (the slide should feel warm, not hot).
Flood with crystal violet for 1 minute; rinse gently with water.
Flood with Gram's iodine for 1 minute; rinse gently with water.
Decolourise with 95% ethanol added drop by drop for 10–30 seconds — stop the moment the run-off turns clear.
Rinse immediately with water to halt decolourisation.
Counterstain with safranin for 30–60 seconds; rinse and blot dry (do not rub).
Examine under oil immersion (100×): Gram-positive cells appear purple/violet, Gram-negative cells pink/red.
Record cell shape, arrangement and Gram reaction; clean the objective with lens tissue afterwards.
protocols.note: Use only young cultures — old Gram-positive cells decolourise and read falsely Gram-negative. Over-decolourisation is the commonest error; run known Gram-positive and Gram-negative controls alongside doubtful samples. Most plant-pathogenic bacteria (Xanthomonas, Pseudomonas, Ralstonia, Pectobacterium) are Gram-negative; Clavibacter and Streptomyces are Gram-positive.

protocols.name: Isolation of bacterial plant pathogens (ooze & streak)
protocols.pr: Bacteria stream out of cut vascular or lesion tissue into water; streaking this suspension on nutrient medium separates single colonies for purification.
mat: Sterile distilled water in small tubes/watch glass
Nutrient agar / NA-glucose or a semi-selective medium
Sterile plates, inoculation loop, spirit lamp, laminar air flow
st: Wash the diseased tissue under running water; select pieces from the junction of healthy and infected tissue.
Surface-disinfect briefly — wipe with 70% ethanol or dip 30 s in 0.5–1% hypochlorite — then rinse in sterile water.
Cut 2–5 mm pieces and place them in a small volume of sterile distilled water.
Stand for 10–20 minutes to allow bacterial ooze; a milky cloud streaming from the cut end confirms bacterial involvement (verify under the microscope).
Take a loopful of the suspension and streak by the quadrant method on nutrient agar, flaming and cooling the loop between quadrants.
Incubate at 28 ± 2 °C for 24–48 h; hold slow growers up to 5–7 days before discarding as negative.
Pick well-separated single colonies, note colony colour, margin, elevation and mucoid character, and re-streak to purify.
Maintain the pure culture on nutrient agar slants at 4 °C and confirm identity by Gram reaction, KOH test and biochemical or molecular methods.
protocols.note: Bacteria sit on and just under the surface — over-sterilising the tissue kills the pathogen. Fungal overgrowth can be suppressed with cycloheximide. Always confirm pathogenicity by re-inoculating a healthy host.

protocols.name: KOH solubility test (rapid Gram differentiation)
protocols.pr: 3% KOH lyses the thin wall of Gram-negative bacteria, releasing DNA that makes the suspension viscous and stringy; Gram-positive cells resist lysis and the suspension stays watery.
st: Place a drop of 3% KOH on a clean slide.
Pick a loopful of a 24 h culture and mix it into the drop for 5–10 seconds.
Lift the loop slowly, 1–2 cm above the slide, and watch the suspension.
A viscous thread that follows the loop indicates a Gram-negative organism; a watery drop that does not string indicates Gram-positive.
Record the result alongside the Gram stain — the two should agree.
protocols.note: KOH is corrosive — gloves, and rinse any skin contact with plenty of water. Use fresh 3% KOH; older solutions give weak reactions. This test complements, rather than replaces, the Gram stain.

protocols.name: Hypersensitive reaction (HR) test on tobacco
protocols.pr: Most plant-pathogenic bacteria elicit rapid, confluent tissue collapse when infiltrated into a non-host leaf, distinguishing pathogens from saprophytes.
mat: Sterile distilled water or 10 mM phosphate buffer
Healthy tobacco plants (Nicotiana tabacum) at 6–8 leaf stage
st: Prepare a dense bacterial suspension in sterile water (approximately 10⁸ cfu/mL — faintly turbid).
Select a healthy, fully expanded tobacco leaf; support the underside with a finger.
Press the needleless syringe against the lower leaf surface and infiltrate gently until a water-soaked patch spreads (about 1 cm²).
Infiltrate a sterile water or buffer patch on the same leaf as a negative control; mark all patches.
Keep the plants in a glasshouse at 25–30 °C and observe at 12, 24 and 48 h.
A positive HR is confluent collapse and drying of the infiltrated patch within 24–48 h, sharply limited to the infiltrated area; the control patch stays green.
protocols.note: Softly rotting bacteria (Pectobacterium) may macerate rather than give a typical HR. A negative result does not by itself prove non-pathogenicity — confirm on the natural host.

protocols.name: Micrometry — measuring microscopic structures
protocols.pr: An ocular micrometer scale in the eyepiece is calibrated against a stage micrometer of known divisions; the calibration factor for each objective then converts ocular divisions into micrometres.
mat: Stage micrometer (1 mm divided into 100 divisions, i.e. 10 μm each)
Prepared slide of the structures to be measured
st: Insert the ocular micrometer disc into the eyepiece, scale side up.
Place the stage micrometer on the stage and focus at 10×.
Rotate the eyepiece and move the stage until the two scales lie parallel with their left-hand lines coinciding.
Find a point further along where a line of the ocular scale coincides exactly with a line of the stage scale.
Count the ocular divisions (OD) and stage divisions (SD) between the two coinciding points.
Calibration factor = (SD × 10) / OD μm per ocular division — since each stage division is 10 μm.
Repeat the calibration separately for 40× and 100×; the factor is different for every objective.
Replace the stage micrometer with the specimen slide, measure the structure in ocular divisions and multiply by the calibration factor for that objective.
Measure at least 25–50 structures per isolate and report mean ± SD with the range.
protocols.note: Recalibrate whenever the eyepiece, objective or microscope changes — factors are not transferable between instruments. Record the objective used with every measurement; a set of measurements without its magnification is unusable data.

protocols.name: Serial dilution & CFU counting (dilution plating)
protocols.pr: A suspension is diluted in known steps until colonies are countable; each colony arises from one viable propagule, so the count multiplied by the dilution factor gives the population in the original sample.
mat: Sample (soil, plant extract, bioagent formulation or culture suspension)
Sterile distilled water blanks (9 mL each)
Nutrient agar / PDA / selective medium plates
Sterile pipettes or micropipette with sterile tips
Vortex mixer, L-shaped spreader, laminar air flow
st: Weigh 1 g of sample (or take 1 mL of suspension) into 9 mL sterile water and vortex thoroughly — this is the 10⁻¹ dilution.
Transfer 1 mL from this tube into the next 9 mL blank and vortex; repeat to obtain 10⁻² to 10⁻⁶ as required (see the dilution diagram).
Use a fresh sterile tip for every transfer and vortex before each one — settled propagules give false low counts.

Pipette 0.1 mL of the chosen dilutions onto pre-dried plates; spread evenly with a sterile spreader (spread plate). For the pour-plate method, add 1 mL to the plate and pour molten medium cooled to ~45 °C.
Plate at least three replications per dilution, and include an uninoculated plate as a sterility control.
Incubate: bacteria 28 ± 2 °C for 24–48 h; fungi 25 ± 2 °C for 3–5 days.
Select plates bearing 30–300 colonies for bacteria (or 10–100 for fungi) — counts outside this range are statistically unreliable.
Count the colonies, average the replications, and calculate: CFU/mL or CFU/g = (mean count × dilution factor) / volume plated. Use the CFU tool in the Calculators tab.
Report the count together with the medium used, incubation temperature and time.
protocols.note: Express soil counts on an oven-dry weight basis by running a separate moisture estimation. Spreading before the surface is dry causes colonies to run together; pre-dry plates in the cabinet for 15 min. Record the dilution actually counted — a CFU value without its dilution factor cannot be checked.

protocols.name: LOPAT tests for fluorescent Pseudomonas identification
protocols.pr: Five determinative tests — Levan production, Oxidase, Pectolytic activity, Arginine dihydrolase and Tobacco hypersensitivity — separate fluorescent pseudomonads into five groups, distinguishing plant pathogens from saprophytes.
mat: 24–48 h pure culture on nutrient agar
Kovács oxidase reagent (1% tetramethyl-p-phenylenediamine dihydrochloride) or oxidase discs
Fresh potato slices in sterile Petri dishes (pectolytic test)
Thornley's arginine medium in tubes with sterile liquid paraffin
Tobacco plants at 6–8 leaf stage, needleless syringe
Inoculation loop, spirit lamp, filter paper
st: L — Levan: streak the culture on nutrient agar containing 5% sucrose; incubate 48–72 h at 28 °C. Large, white, domed, mucoid colonies indicate levan production (+).

O — Oxidase: smear a loopful of a young culture on filter paper moistened with Kovács reagent (or use a commercial disc). A deep purple colour within 10–30 seconds is positive (+); ignore colour appearing later.

P — Pectolytic activity: place scrubbed, surface-sterilised potato slices in sterile plates on moist filter paper; stab-inoculate the centre and incubate at 28 °C for 48–72 h. Soft, macerated, sunken tissue is positive (+).

A — Arginine dihydrolase: stab Thornley's arginine medium, overlay with sterile liquid paraffin to exclude air, and incubate up to 7 days. A change from orange to red/pink indicates a positive reaction (+).
T — Tobacco hypersensitivity: infiltrate a dense suspension (≈10⁸ cfu/mL) into a tobacco leaf (see the HR protocol). Confluent collapse within 24–48 h is positive (+).
Run all five tests on the same culture, with known positive and negative reference strains alongside.
Read the pattern against the LOPAT group table to assign the isolate to Groups I–V.
Confirm the identification by pathogenicity on the natural host and, where available, by 16S rDNA or species-specific PCR.
protocols.note: LOPAT is presumptive, not confirmatory — it places an isolate in a group; species and pathovar identity need host pathogenicity and molecular confirmation. Use young cultures throughout; old cells give unreliable oxidase and levan reactions. Never read the oxidase test after 30 seconds.

protocols.name: Bacterial ooze (streaming) test
protocols.pr: Bacteria in infected vascular or lesion tissue stream out in visible threads when a cut section is suspended in water, giving a rapid field or bench indication of bacterial infection.
mat: Freshly wilted or lesioned plant material
Clean glass slide, coverslip, or a clear glass/test tube of water
st: Select a stem, petiole or leaf showing fresh symptoms; wilting plants are best sampled at the collar or lower stem.
Cut a 2–5 cm section with a clean blade, avoiding crushed or dried tissue.
Glass test version: suspend the cut section vertically in a glass of clear water so the cut end is just submerged, and observe against a dark background without disturbing the water.
A milky-white thread streaming downward from the cut end within 1–5 minutes is a positive ooze test — typical of Ralstonia solanacearum in solanaceous wilt.
Slide version: place a thin section in a drop of water on a slide, apply a coverslip and examine at 10× and 40× for bacterial streaming from the cut vascular bundles.
Follow a positive result by isolation on nutrient agar or a semi-selective medium; the ooze test alone does not identify the species.
protocols.note: Fungal wilts (Fusarium, Verticillium) and physiological wilt give no ooze — which is exactly what makes this test useful in the field. Use clear, still water and a dark background; turbid water masks the thread.

protocols.name: Oxidative–Fermentative (Hugh & Leifson) test
protocols.pr: Growth with acid production in an open tube only indicates oxidative metabolism; acid in both open and sealed (anaerobic) tubes indicates fermentation — a key separation among plant-pathogenic bacteria.
mat: Hugh & Leifson O–F medium with 1% glucose and bromothymol blue
st: Prepare two tubes of O–F medium per isolate.
Stab-inoculate both tubes with a straight needle to about two-thirds of the depth.
Overlay one tube with 1–2 cm sterile liquid paraffin (closed/anaerobic); leave the second open (aerobic).
Incubate at 28 ± 2 °C and examine daily for up to 7–14 days.
Yellow (acid) in the open tube only = oxidative (e.g. Pseudomonas, Xanthomonas).
Yellow in both tubes = fermentative (e.g. Pectobacterium, Dickeya and other Enterobacteriaceae).
No colour change in either = non-saccharolytic (inert).
Always include an uninoculated pair as a control.
protocols.note: Use a needle, not a loop, so the stab channel stays narrow. Paraffin must be sterile and deep enough — a thin layer lets air in and gives a false fermentative reading.

protocols.name: Starch hydrolysis test
protocols.pr: Amylase-producing bacteria hydrolyse starch in the medium; iodine then stains the residual starch blue-black, leaving a clear halo around hydrolysing colonies.
mat: Starch agar plates (nutrient agar + 0.2–0.5% soluble starch)
st: Streak or spot-inoculate the isolate on starch agar; include a known amylase-positive control.
Incubate at 28 ± 2 °C for 48–72 h until good growth develops.
Flood the plate with iodine solution and read immediately.
A clear, colourless halo around the growth against a blue-black background is positive (+); uniform blue-black up to the colony margin is negative (−).
Discard the plate after reading — iodine-flooded plates cannot be re-incubated.
protocols.note: Most Xanthomonas species are starch-hydrolysis positive, which helps separate them from fluorescent pseudomonads. Read within a minute; the halo fades as iodine diffuses.

protocols.name: Phytophthora baiting from soil and water
protocols.pr: Zoospores released in flooded soil or in water are attracted to susceptible plant tissue floated on the surface; the pathogen colonises the bait, from which it is easily isolated.
mat: Clean plastic tray or beaker, sterile distilled water
Baits: young leaves (rhododendron, Persea, citrus), green pear or apple fruit, or leaf discs
Selective medium (PARP / P₁₀VP: pimaricin, ampicillin, rifampicin, PCNB)
Sterile blade, blotting paper, incubator at 20–25 °C
st: Place 100–200 g of soil in a tray and flood with sterile distilled water to 2–3 cm above the soil surface; for water samples use the sample directly.
Float the baits on the water surface — leaf discs, whole young leaves, or a wounded green fruit half-submerged.
Incubate at 20–25 °C in diffuse light for 2–5 days; avoid disturbance.
Examine the baits daily for water-soaked, brown lesions spreading from the margins or the wound.
Blot the lesioned bait dry, cut small pieces from the advancing lesion margin, and plate on PARP selective medium.
Incubate at 25 °C in the dark and examine after 2–4 days for coenocytic, non-septate hyphae with characteristic branching.
Confirm by inducing sporangia in non-sterile soil extract or pond water, and by ITS sequencing.
protocols.note: Baiting detects only viable, zoospore-producing propagules — a negative result is not proof of absence. Fruit baiting (green pear or apple) is the more sensitive method for species that sporulate poorly on leaves; keep the temperature below 28 °C, as most Phytophthora species stop sporulating above it.

protocols.name: Pythium baiting (grass blade / hemp seed)
protocols.pr: Pythium zoospores in flooded soil rapidly colonise fine, susceptible baits such as grass leaf blades or hemp seed, which can then be plated onto selective medium.
mat: Sterile distilled water, plastic trays or Petri dishes
Baits: sterilised grass leaf blades, hemp (Cannabis) seed, or cucumber/sesame seed
Water agar and selective medium (PARP or CMA + antibiotics)
st: Place 20–50 g soil in a dish and flood with sterile distilled water 2 cm above the soil.
Add the baits: cut sterilised grass blades 1–2 cm long, or pre-soaked hemp seeds, floated on the surface.
Incubate at 25 °C for 24–48 h — Pythium colonises much faster than Phytophthora.
Remove baits, rinse in sterile water, blot dry and plate onto water agar or PARP.
Examine after 24 h for fast-growing, aseptate hyphae; transfer hyphal tips to corn meal agar for purification.
Induce sporangia and oogonia in sterile soil extract water for morphological identification.
protocols.note: Bait within 24–48 h — leaving the setup longer lets Pythium and bacteria overrun everything. Hyphal-tip transfer from the advancing margin gives cleaner cultures than plating bait pieces alone.

protocols.name: Rhizoctonia solani baiting from soil
protocols.pr: Rhizoctonia grows from soil onto susceptible bait tissue placed in contact with moist soil, allowing recovery without dilution plating, which the fungus survives poorly.
mat: Baits: beet seed, toothpicks/wooden matchsticks, or radish/mustard seedlings
Water agar or PDA with streptomycin
st: Moisten the soil sample to about field capacity and pack it into a container.
Insert the baits: sterilised toothpicks pushed vertically into the soil, or bury pre-soaked beet seeds 1 cm deep.
Incubate at 25 °C for 3–7 days, keeping the soil moist but not waterlogged.
Retrieve the baits, rinse free of soil, surface-disinfect briefly and blot dry.
Plate on water agar or antibiotic-amended PDA and incubate at 25 °C.
Identify by right-angle branching with a septum and constriction near the branch origin, and multinucleate cells (stain with safranin–KOH or aniline blue).
Determine the anastomosis group by pairing with tester isolates on water agar.
protocols.note: Rhizoctonia does not survive soil dilution plating well — baiting is the method of choice. Keep the soil moist but never flooded, or Pythium takes over the baits.

protocols.name: Sclerotial recovery from soil (Macrophomina, Sclerotium, Sclerotinia)
protocols.pr: Sclerotia are separated from soil by wet sieving and flotation and then plated on a selective medium, giving a quantitative estimate of inoculum density.
mat: Selective medium (chloroneb–mercuric chloride–rose bengal for Macrophomina, or PDA + streptomycin)
Blotting paper, stereo microscope, incubator at 30 °C for Macrophomina
st: Air-dry the soil, sieve out stones and debris, and weigh a known quantity (typically 10–25 g).
Suspend in water and wash through nested sieves; sclerotia are retained on the finer sieve while clay and silt pass through.
Back-wash the retained fraction into a beaker; surface-disinfect in 0.5% sodium hypochlorite for 1–2 min and rinse in three changes of sterile water.
Spread the washings on blotting paper and, if required, pick sclerotia under the stereo microscope by size and colour.
Plate the fraction on the selective medium; incubate at 30 ± 2 °C for Macrophomina (25 °C for Sclerotium/Sclerotinia) for 3–5 days.
Count the colonies arising and express inoculum density as sclerotia (cfu) per gram of oven-dry soil.
Confirm identity from colony characters and sclerotial morphology; measure sclerotia by micrometry where variability is being studied.
protocols.note: Report on an oven-dry soil basis — run a separate moisture estimation on the same sample. Recovery efficiency differs between soil types, so compare treatments only within one soil. Handle mercuric-chloride-amended media with the precautions in the Chemicals tab.

protocols.name: Carnation Leaf Agar (CLA) for Fusarium sporulation
protocols.pr: Sterile carnation leaf pieces on a nutrient-poor agar induce Fusarium to form typical macroconidia in sporodochia, which are essential for morphological identification.
mat: Carnation leaf pieces (5 mm, from plants grown without fungicide), gamma- or autoclave-sterilised
st: Place 2–3 sterile carnation leaf pieces on the surface of a water agar plate.
Inoculate the agar beside a leaf piece with a small mycelial block from the culture margin.
Incubate at 25 °C under alternating 12 h near-UV/dark for 7–14 days.
Examine the leaf pieces for orange-cream sporodochia; mount spores in lactophenol cotton blue.
Record macroconidial shape, septation, apical and basal cell form, presence of microconidia, phialide type and chlamydospores.
Measure at least 25–50 macroconidia by micrometry and compare with standard keys.
protocols.note: Fusarium on PDA degenerates rapidly into sterile pale mycelium (‘pionnotal' growth) and cannot be identified reliably — CLA is the reference substrate. Always identify from CLA, never from PDA morphology alone.

protocols.name: Catalase test
protocols.pr: Catalase-producing bacteria break down hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen, seen as immediate effervescence.
mat: Clean glass slide, wooden applicator or loop
st: Place a drop of 3% H₂O₂ on a clean slide.
Using a wooden applicator or a cooled loop, pick a small amount of a 24 h culture and mix into the drop.
Observe immediately: brisk, sustained bubbling within 5–10 seconds is positive (+).
No bubbles, or a few scattered bubbles only, is negative (−).
Run known positive and negative controls with every batch.
protocols.note: Never pick colonies from blood-containing media — red cells contain catalase and give false positives. Use fresh H₂O₂; it decomposes on storage. A nichrome loop can also give false bubbling, so a wooden stick is safer.

protocols.name: Kovács indole test
protocols.pr: Bacteria possessing tryptophanase convert tryptophan to indole, which forms a red ring with Kovács reagent.
mat: Kovács reagent (p-dimethylaminobenzaldehyde in amyl alcohol and HCl)
st: Inoculate 5 mL tryptone broth with the test isolate.
Incubate at 28 ± 2 °C for 24–48 h (up to 96 h for slow growers).
Add 0.5 mL Kovács reagent down the side of the tube without shaking.
Read within one minute: a cherry-red ring at the surface is positive (+); a yellow layer is negative (−).
Include an uninoculated broth as a control.
protocols.note: Kovács reagent contains HCl and amyl alcohol — handle in a ventilated area, gloves on. Do not shake the tube; the colour develops in the alcohol layer at the surface.

protocols.name: Nitrate reduction test
protocols.pr: Nitrate reductase converts nitrate to nitrite, detected as a red colour with sulphanilic acid and α-naphthylamine; zinc dust then distinguishes complete reduction from no reduction at all.
mat: Nitrate broth (peptone + 0.1% KNO₃), Durham tubes optional
Reagent A: sulphanilic acid in acetic acid
Reagent B: α-naphthylamine in acetic acid
st: Inoculate nitrate broth and incubate at 28 ± 2 °C for 24–48 h; keep an uninoculated tube as control.
Add 3–5 drops each of reagents A and B.
A red colour within 1–2 minutes indicates nitrite present — nitrate reduction positive (+).
If no colour develops, add a small pinch of zinc dust and wait 5–10 minutes.
Red colour after zinc = nitrate still present, so the organism did NOT reduce it (−).
No colour even after zinc = nitrate was reduced beyond nitrite (to N₂ or NH₃) — still positive (+).
protocols.note: α-Naphthylamine is a suspected carcinogen — gloves, and dispose of reagents as chemical waste. The zinc confirmation step is essential; skipping it turns a strong positive into a recorded negative.

protocols.name: Gelatin liquefaction test
protocols.pr: Gelatinase-producing bacteria hydrolyse gelatin, which then fails to re-solidify on chilling.
st: Stab-inoculate a nutrient gelatin tube to about two-thirds depth; keep one uninoculated as control.
Incubate at 28 ± 2 °C for up to 7–14 days.
Refrigerate both tubes at 4 °C for 30 minutes.
Liquid (unsolidified) medium after chilling indicates gelatin hydrolysis (+); a firm gel is negative (−).
Re-incubate negatives and re-test weekly up to 14 days before finalising.
protocols.note: Always chill the control alongside — gelatin that fails to set for other reasons would otherwise be read as positive. Read promptly; tubes left at room temperature liquefy on their own.

protocols.name: Citrate utilisation test
protocols.pr: Organisms able to use citrate as the sole carbon source raise the medium pH, turning the bromothymol blue indicator from green to blue.
st: Streak the slant surface lightly with a needle carrying a light inoculum — do not stab the butt.
Incubate at 28 ± 2 °C for 24–48 h (up to 7 days for slow growers), caps loosened for aeration.
A change from green to Prussian blue, usually with visible growth, is positive (+).
Medium remaining green with no growth is negative (−).
protocols.note: Use a light inoculum from a plate, never from a nutrient broth — carried-over nutrients allow growth without citrate use and give false positives. Caps must be loose; the test is strictly aerobic.

protocols.name: Urease test
protocols.pr: Urease hydrolyses urea to ammonia, raising the pH and turning the phenol red indicator pink.
st: Streak the urea agar slant heavily over the whole surface.
Incubate at 28 ± 2 °C with the cap loose; examine at 6 h, 24 h and up to 7 days.
A bright pink-magenta colour indicates urease activity (+).
Yellow-orange (unchanged) is negative (−).
Include an uninoculated slant as control.
protocols.note: Record the time of the reaction — rapid urease producers turn the slant pink within hours, while weak producers take days, and the distinction is diagnostically useful.

protocols.name: Levan production (5% sucrose) test
protocols.pr: On sucrose-rich medium, levansucrase-producing bacteria form the polysaccharide levan, giving large, white, domed, mucoid colonies. This is the 'L' of LOPAT.
st: Streak the isolate onto nutrient agar containing 5% sucrose to obtain well-separated colonies.
Incubate at 28 ± 2 °C for 48–72 h.
Large (3–5 mm), white, domed, glistening and mucoid colonies indicate levan production (+).
Flat, translucent, non-mucoid colonies are negative (−).
Compare against growth of the same isolate on plain nutrient agar.
protocols.note: Read at 48–72 h; earlier readings miss the domed character and later ones dry out. Some non-levan bacteria are mucoid from other polysaccharides, so read it together with the rest of LOPAT.

protocols.name: Potato slice (pectolytic activity) test
protocols.pr: Pectolytic bacteria macerate potato tissue by degrading pectin in the middle lamella, producing a soft, sunken rot. This is the 'P' of LOPAT.
mat: Sterile Petri dishes with moist filter paper
st: Wash, peel and surface-disinfect the tuber; cut 5–8 mm slices with a sterile blade.
Place each slice in a sterile Petri dish on moistened sterile filter paper to maintain humidity.
Stab-inoculate the centre of the slice with a loopful of the culture; keep an uninoculated slice as control.
Incubate at 28 ± 2 °C for 24–72 h.
Soft, watery, macerated tissue that collapses when tilted is positive (+); firm tissue with only surface growth is negative (−).
protocols.note: Keep the humidity high but do not flood the dish — free water spreads bacteria and confuses the reading. Discoloration alone is not maceration; test the tissue with a needle tip.

protocols.name: Arginine dihydrolase (Thornley's) test
protocols.pr: Arginine dihydrolase releases ammonia under anaerobic conditions, raising the pH and turning Thornley's medium from orange to red. This is the 'A' of LOPAT.
st: Stab-inoculate Thornley's medium to the bottom of the tube.
Overlay with 1–2 cm sterile liquid paraffin to exclude oxygen.
Incubate at 28 ± 2 °C and examine daily for up to 7 days.
A change from orange to red or pink is positive (+); orange or yellow is negative (−).
Include an uninoculated overlaid tube as control.
protocols.note: The paraffin seal must be unbroken — an aerobic tube gives a false negative. Groups IV and V of LOPAT are arginine-positive, which is what separates the saprophytes from the pathogens.

protocols.name: Cobb's sieving and decanting (nematode extraction from soil)
protocols.pr: Nematodes suspended by stirring settle more slowly than soil particles, so successive decanting through graded sieves concentrates them for counting.
mat: Modified Baermann funnel or extraction tray
st: Mix the composite sample thoroughly and take a 250 g sub-sample.
Suspend the soil in about 2 L of water in a bucket; stir vigorously and let the heavy particles settle for 20–30 seconds.
Decant the suspension through a 20-mesh sieve (to remove debris) onto a 60-mesh sieve, then onto 100, 200 and 325-mesh sieves in turn.
Repeat the suspension and decanting two or three times to improve recovery.
Back-wash the material retained on the finer sieves (200 and 325 mesh) into a beaker.
Transfer the suspension onto a modified Baermann funnel or extraction tray lined with tissue and leave 24–48 h for the nematodes to migrate through.
Collect the clear suspension beneath, concentrate to a known volume, and count in a counting dish under the stereo microscope.
Express the population as nematodes per 200 g (or per kg) of soil, noting genus where identifiable.
protocols.note: Recovery falls sharply in heavy clay soils — compare treatments only within one soil type. Do not let the sample dry before extraction, and process within 24–48 h of sampling.

protocols.name: Baermann funnel technique (nematode extraction from soil or tissue)
protocols.pr: Active nematodes migrate out of the sample through tissue paper and settle in the funnel stem, separating them from debris.
mat: Glass funnel with rubber tubing and pinch clip
Soil sample or chopped root/plant tissue
st: Fit rubber tubing with a pinch clip to the funnel stem and fill the funnel with water.
Line a sieve or basket with two layers of tissue paper and place it in the funnel so the base just contacts the water.
Spread 50–100 g of soil, or 5–10 g of chopped roots, evenly on the tissue.
Add water gently until the sample is just moistened and in contact with the water below — do not submerge it.
Leave undisturbed at room temperature for 24–48 h.
Open the clip and draw off 10–15 mL from the stem into a counting dish.
Count under the stereo microscope; kill and fix with hot 4% formalin if the specimens are to be kept.
protocols.note: Only active nematodes are recovered, so eggs and inactive stages are missed. Do not exceed 48 h — oxygen depletion kills the nematodes and they sink out of the collection zone.

protocols.name: Root-knot nematode: root staining and gall indexing
protocols.pr: Acid fuchsin stains nematodes inside root tissue, allowing females, juveniles and egg masses to be seen and infection to be scored.
mat: Infected roots, washed free of soil
st: Wash roots gently free of soil and cut into 1–2 cm pieces.
For egg-mass counting, immerse whole roots in 0.015% phloxine B for 15–20 minutes; egg masses stain pink and are counted under the stereo microscope.
For internal staining, soak root pieces in 1–1.5% NaOCl for 4 minutes to clear, then rinse thoroughly in running water for 45 seconds.
Boil the roots in acid fuchsin solution for 30 seconds, then cool.
Destain in acidified glycerol until the roots are clear and the nematodes stand out red.
Examine under the stereo microscope; count females, juveniles and egg masses per root system.
Score galling on the 0–5 scale (0 = no galls; 1 = 1–2; 2 = 3–10; 3 = 11–30; 4 = 31–100; 5 = more than 100 galls per root system).
protocols.note: Sodium hypochlorite for more than 4 minutes destroys root tissue — time it. Record the scale used with the score, as several gall-index scales exist and results are not comparable between them.

protocols.name: Indicator (assay) host inoculation for virus identification
protocols.pr: Diagnostic host plants respond to particular viruses with characteristic local or systemic symptoms, giving a bioassay-based provisional identification.
mat: Indicator hosts raised in an insect-proof glasshouse
st: Raise indicator hosts to the correct stage: Chenopodium amaranticolor and C. quinoa (local lesions for many viruses), Nicotiana glutinosa and N. tabacum cv. Xanthi (local lesions for TMV), N. benthamiana (broad systemic host), Datura metel, cowpea cv. C-152 (local lesions for many begomo- and potyviruses), and the natural host as a check.
Prepare sap in chilled buffer as in the sap-inoculation protocol.
Dust the leaves with carborundum and inoculate 2–3 leaves per plant, keeping buffer-only controls.
Rinse the leaves after 2–5 minutes and label every plant with isolate, host and date.
Maintain at 25–30 °C in an insect-proof glasshouse.
Record local lesions at 3–7 days (type, colour, size, number) and systemic symptoms at 7–21 days (mosaic, mottling, vein clearing, leaf distortion, necrosis).
Compare the symptom pattern across the host range with published descriptions, and confirm by ELISA or PCR.
protocols.note: Symptom expression is strongly affected by temperature and light — keep conditions uniform and always include a known positive isolate. Bioassay gives a provisional identification only; sequence or serological confirmation is required for a claim of identity.

protocols.name: Local lesion assay (virus quantification)
protocols.pr: The number of local lesions on a hypersensitive host is proportional to infective virus concentration, allowing relative titres to be compared.
mat: Local-lesion host (Chenopodium amaranticolor, N. glutinosa, cowpea C-152)
st: Raise uniform plants and select fully expanded leaves of comparable age.
Prepare the dilution series of the virus preparation in chilled buffer.
Use the half-leaf method: inoculate one half of each leaf with the test preparation and the other half with the standard, alternating sides between leaves to remove positional bias.
Dust with carborundum, inoculate with uniform pressure, and rinse after 2–5 minutes.
Incubate at 25 °C and count lesions at 3–7 days when they are fully expanded but not coalescing.
Average lesion counts across at least 5–10 leaves per treatment and compare treatments statistically.
protocols.note: Leaf age, position and inoculation pressure all alter lesion number — the half-leaf design controls most of this variation and should always be used for comparisons. Counts above about 100 lesions per half-leaf coalesce and become unreliable; dilute further.

protocols.name: Agar plate method for seed health testing
protocols.pr: Seeds plated on nutrient agar allow seed-borne fungi to grow out and be identified from colony and spore characters, complementing the blotter method.
mat: 1% sodium hypochlorite (for surface disinfection where internal infection is being assessed)
PDA or malt extract agar with streptomycin
Sterile plates, forceps, laminar air flow
st: Divide the sample: one set untreated (total infection), one set surface-disinfected in 1% NaOCl for 2 min and rinsed (internal infection only).
Plate 10 seeds per 9 cm plate, evenly spaced, on antibiotic-amended agar; 400 seeds per sample as per ISTA.
Incubate at 22 ± 2 °C under alternating 12 h light/dark for 5–7 days.
Examine colonies growing from each seed; identify from colony characters and slide mounts.
Record per cent seed infection for each fungus, separately for treated and untreated sets.
The difference between the two sets estimates the proportion of externally borne inoculum.
protocols.note: The agar method detects slow-growing and internally borne fungi that the blotter method misses, but fast saprophytes can overrun the plates — read from day 4 onwards rather than waiting the full period.

protocols.name: Slide culture technique
protocols.pr: A fungus grown between a slide and coverslip on a thin agar block can be examined undisturbed, preserving the natural arrangement of conidiophores and spores.
mat: Sterile Petri dish with moist filter paper and a bent glass rod
Thin PDA or water agar blocks (1 cm square)
st: Assemble a moist chamber: bent glass rod on filter paper in a Petri dish, with a sterile slide resting on the rod; sterilise the assembly.
Place a 1 cm square agar block on the slide.
Inoculate all four edges of the block with a minute amount of the fungus.
Place a sterile coverslip over the block and moisten the filter paper with sterile water.
Incubate at 25 ± 2 °C for 3–7 days until sporulation is visible at the block edges.
Lift the coverslip, place it on a drop of lactophenol cotton blue on a fresh slide, and examine — a second mount can be made from the agar-side growth on the original slide.
Seal with nail varnish for a semi-permanent preparation.
protocols.note: A drop of 95% ethanol on the coverslip before mounting wets the hydrophobic spores of Aspergillus and Penicillium. Do not let the moist chamber dry out during incubation.
